paras: The lynching of Frank Fisher took place on Sunday afternoon, April 30, 1882, at Galion, Crawford County, Ohio, when a crowd broke into the City Hall prison, took out Fisher, a Black man accused of raping a thirteen-year-old girl, and hanged him in nearby woods. He protested his innocence to the end. Ohio papers remarked that it was done by unmasked men, in daylight, on a Sunday, before thousands of onlookers.

On Friday, April 28, Barbara Rettig, a German girl of thirteen, was reported to have been assaulted in the woods near her home outside Galion. Wires dated April 29 said several hundred men were searching for the accused man, there named "Jerry Myers" (a Napoleon, Ohio, brief later called him "Frank Smith"), and that "if found he will be lynched."

According to the Galion correspondent of the Cleveland Herald, officers T. J. Wurts and W. H. W. Nichols arrested Frank Fisher about 5 a.m. on April 30 at Fredericktown, Knox County, as he was leaving on foot. He reached Galion by carriage at 11:30 and was locked in an iron cage in the City Hall prison while officials planned to move him to the county jail at Bucyrus or another county for fear of lynching.

At about 3 p.m. an unmasked crowd carrying hammers, crowbars and a rope gathered at the prison and demanded Fisher. The officers refused, and Mayor Underwood, G. M. Zeigler and others urged the crowd to let the law take its course, without effect. The crowd forced the doors, broke open the cage and pulled Fisher into the street; the Cincinnati Commercial's correspondent wrote that "a negro broke open the cell."

The crowd then marched Fisher to the house at the foot of South Market Street, just south of the city limits, where the girl was reported to have said, "That is the man who did it," and fainted. He was then taken to the nearby woods where the assault was said to have occurred.

There he was allowed a short prayer, reported as "O Lord, take care of me. I know that I am going to die, but I have many friends," before the crowd's shouts drowned him out. He was hanged with the rope fastened to a stump at 4:10, before at least 2,000 men, women and children, many from neighboring towns, and the body still hung at 9 p.m.

The Herald correspondent wrote that the coroner had been notified and that there was "some talk" of indicting the leaders, but that it "would not be safe to attempt that at present"; no verdict or indictment appears in the coverage. Local opinion was reported both ways: the Commercial's correspondent wrote that many in Galion condemned the lynching, while a Galion special of May 1 said few condemned it and the general sentiment was that it was "well done."

The white press carried the April 29 manhunt wires and then the April 30 Cleveland and Cincinnati dispatches, which ran the next day from Washington to Sacramento. Distant papers reduced the story to a line, naming Fisher as "colored" and the girl as white, while the St. Paul Daily Globe filed it under "The Minneapolis Plan," linking it to a lynching there two days earlier, with the deck "Hung by Indignant Citizens." Papers called him a "ravisher" and a "black beast" and treated his guilt as settled, though they recorded his denial.

Ohio weeklies ran the fullest accounts in the first week of May, several under "Judge Lynch" headings. The Eaton Democrat said the "decision of Judge Lynch" met with "universal approval," and the Herald correspondent wrote that Fisher had no sympathy from anyone. The Somerset Press called the scene "unusual" for Ohio, and by mid-May papers in Kansas and Minnesota counted it among the month's lynchings for rape.

Accounts differ on the size of the crowd, from about 200 men in the Cleveland wire and 300 in an Indianapolis printing to over 2,000 and 4,000 in the Commercial special. The Galion special of May 1 said Fisher was kicked, choked and stoned on the way and hanged over a tree limb, details absent from the Herald correspondent's eyewitness account of a rope tied to a stump.

reader.title: Lynching of Frank Fisher
bases: A crowd broke into the Galion city prison, took out Frank Fisher, a Black man accused of rape, and hanged him in nearby woods (A7, A9, A24).

Fisher was hanged by a crowd numbered from about 200 to several thousand after it forced the prison over the refusal of the officers and the mayor (A9, A13, A24), on the accusation that he had raped a thirteen-year-old girl, which the papers called the 'decision of Judge Lynch' (A20, A24).

Separate accounts from the Cleveland wire (A7, A13), a Cincinnati Commercial special (A9), a Cleveland Herald special (A16, A24) and a Plain Dealer-style Galion special (A21) agree that Fisher was taken from the Galion prison and hanged on April 30.

accounts.label: Pre-capture wire (Galion/Cleveland, Apr. 29)
accounts.gist: Several hundred men were hunting 'Jerry Myers' for the rape of a thirteen-year-old girl, and he would be lynched if found.

accounts.label: Galion correspondent of the Cleveland Herald
accounts.gist: An eyewitness account: an unmasked crowd with hammers, crowbars and a rope broke into the prison at 3 p.m., had the girl identify Fisher at her home, and hanged him in the woods at 4:10 with the rope made fast to a stump, before at least 2,000 people.

accounts.label: Cleveland wire
accounts.gist: A mob of about 200 (or 300) men took Fisher from the prison after the mayor's speeches failed, had him identified, and hanged him; he made no resistance.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Commercial special
accounts.gist: Over 2,000 people answered whistles and fire bells, broke open the jail with negroes in the mob, took Fisher to the girl's bedside and hanged him before 4,000; many in Galion condemned it.

accounts.label: Galion special of May 1 (Ravenna Democratic Press)
accounts.gist: Fisher was dragged through the street, kicked, choked and stoned, shrieked for mercy, and was hanged from a tree limb by a mob of at least 2,000; the body hung all night and sentiment held it 'well done'.

framing.detail: The Eaton Democrat said the 'decision of Judge Lynch' on the 'black beast' met with 'universal approval' and urged that such men be hanged without waiting on the law.
The Cleveland Herald special called Fisher 'as black-hearted a demon as ever trod the earth', said a trial would only 'cheat the gallows', and regretted the affair only mildly.
The St. Paul Daily Globe headlined 'The Minneapolis Plan' and 'Hung by Indignant Citizens'.
The Wheeling Intelligencer headlined 'A Black Fiend Lynched' but carried the Commercial's note that many in Galion condemned it.
The Somerset Press called the scene 'unusual' for Ohio while stating Fisher's guilt as fact.
Distant papers ran one-line telegrams naming Fisher as 'colored' and the girl as white.

conflicts.note: All accounts describe one man; the Herald correspondent says Fisher denied his name on arrest. Fisher is the name in every post-lynching account but one.
